lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Simple Agricultural Tools and the Rules for Handling and Maintaining Them

pages.body:
Visit the school garden or a farm close to your school. Look at the tools that the farmers are using and at how they are stored when the work is over.

- Which tools did you see, and what is each one used for?
- Which tools looked well cared for and which looked neglected? How could you tell?

A farmer who has good tools in good condition can work faster, more safely and with better results. In this lesson we name the simple tools used on crop farms and animal farms, explain what handling and maintenance mean and learn the basic rules for each.

We begin with the tools that are used to prepare land and grow crops.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Simple tools used on crop farms

pages.title: Simple tools used on crop farms
pages.body:
| **Tool** | **Main use** |
|---|---|
| Cutlass | Clearing bush, cutting weeds and harvesting crops such as plantain and cassava |
| Hoe | Weeding, making mounds and ridges, and loosening soil |
| Pickaxe | Breaking hard or stony ground and digging holes |
| Shovel and spade | Digging, lifting and moving soil, compost and manure |
| Rake | Levelling soil, making seedbeds and collecting dry grass or stones |
| Trowel and hand fork | Digging small holes, transplanting seedlings and loosening soil around young plants |
| Dibber | Making small holes for seeds and seedlings |
| Watering can and bucket | Watering seedlings and small plots |
| Wheelbarrow | Carrying soil, manure, harvested crops and other loads |
| Sickle and secateurs | Cutting grass or crops and pruning branches and stems |
| Knapsack sprayer | Spraying water soluble chemicals on crops |
| Measuring tape and line with pegs | Spacing plants and marking out beds in straight lines |
Next we list tools that are used when animals are kept.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Simple tools used on animal farms

pages.title: Simple tools used on animal farms
pages.body:
- Feeders and feeding troughs, which hold feed for animals and poultry.
- Drinkers and drinking troughs, which provide clean water.
- Brooms, rakes and shovels, which are used to clean pens and remove droppings.
- Buckets and wheelbarrows, which are used to carry water, feed and waste.
- Cutlasses, used for cutting fodder, grass and green leaves.
- Ropes and tethers, which keep grazing animals such as goats in place.
- Egg trays and crates, used to collect and carry eggs and birds.

[[pic: Picture board of simple farm tools. One section shows crop tools such as a cutlass, hoe, rake, shovel, trowel and watering can. Another section shows animal tools such as a feeder, a drinker, a bucket and a wheelbarrow. Each tool has its name written beside it.]]

Now we explain two important words and why they matter.

pages.title: What handling and maintenance mean
pages.body:
Handling is the way a tool is held, used, carried and put down. Maintenance is all the care given to a tool to keep it clean, sharp, safe and in good working order. It includes cleaning, drying, sharpening, oiling, repairing and proper storage.

- Good handling prevents injuries to the user and to other people.
- Good maintenance makes tools last longer, so money is saved on replacements.
- Sharp and clean tools do better work with less effort.
- Clean tools used with animals help to stop the spread of disease.
- Tools that are well kept are easy to find and ready when needed.

Here we match the rules of handling and maintenance with the tools they apply to.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Basic rules matched with specific tools

pages.title: Basic rules matched with specific tools
pages.body:
| **Tool** | **Handling rule** | **Maintenance rule** |
|---|---|---|
| Cutlass | Cut away from your body and your legs. Keep other people at a safe distance. Carry it with the blade pointing down | Wash and dry after use. Sharpen with a file or stone. Rub a thin layer of oil on the blade and keep it in a sheath |
| Hoe | Never leave it on the ground with the blade facing up. Keep a firm grip and stand with feet apart | Scrape off soil. Check that the blade is tight on the handle. Oil the metal and keep the handle dry |
| Pickaxe | Swing it slowly in an open area. Make sure no one is close | Check that the head is firm on the handle. Clean and oil the metal |
| Shovel and spade | Bend your knees and lift with your legs. Do not use it to hit things | Wash after use. Remove rust with sand paper. Oil the metal part |
| Rake | Keep the teeth facing down when not in use. Do not leave it with the teeth up | Remove soil and grass from between the teeth. Keep it dry |
| Wheelbarrow | Do not overload it. Push it steadily on level ground | Grease the wheel. Keep the tyre inflated. Wash and dry after use |
| Knapsack sprayer | Wear gloves, a mask and boots. Do not spray against the wind | Rinse the tank thoroughly with clean water after use. Do not leave chemicals in it |
| Secateurs and sickle | Keep blades closed or covered when not in use. Cut away from the hand | Keep blades sharp and oiled |
| Feeders and drinkers | Do not overfill. Keep them off the dirty floor | Wash daily and disinfect often |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: General rules for handling and maintenance

pages.body:
Finally we put the rules together as a short list you can remember.

## General rules for handling and maintenance

1. Use each tool only for the job it was made for.
2. Check the tool before use for loose heads, cracked handles or rust. Do not use a damaged tool.
3. Wear suitable protection such as boots, gloves and goggles for the job.
4. Carry tools with sharp parts pointing down and away from the body, and pass them with the handle facing the other person.
5. Clean tools after each use by removing soil and dirt, washing and drying.
6. Sharpen cutting tools regularly and oil the metal parts to prevent rust.
7. Repair or replace broken handles and loose heads quickly.
8. Store tools in a dry, safe place, such as a tool shed, hung on hooks or racks, and out of the reach of small children.
> **Did you know?** A wooden handle that is kept dry and lightly rubbed with oil lasts much longer than one that is left outside in the rain.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Handling and Maintaining Agricultural Tools in the Community

pages.body:
On the next market day, look at the tools on sale and ask one trader how long a hoe or cutlass lasts. Then ask a farmer what he or she does to make tools last longer.

- What did you learn about the way tools are cared for in your community?
- What is the most common mistake in handling or storing tools that you have seen?

Skills in handling and maintaining tools are best learned by doing. In this lesson we observe tool use on local farms, practise using tools to do simple farm jobs, practise maintaining them and record the rules we find.

We begin by preparing for a visit to a farm in the community and collecting information.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Observing tool use on a farm visit

pages.title: Observing tool use on a farm visit
pages.body:
1. Get permission from the school and from the farmer before the visit and go with your teacher.
2. Prepare an observation sheet with spaces for the name of each tool, its use, how it is handled and how it is kept.
3. During the visit, observe at least five tools in use. Ask polite questions about the care of the tools.
4. Record both good practices and poor practices that you see.
5. Take photographs only if the farmer agrees.

| **Tool** | **Use** | **How it was handled** | **How it was cared for** | **Comment** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Example, hoe | Weeding | Blade facing down when put down | Washed and hung in shed | Good practice |
|  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |

Next we write what we saw as a clear report.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Writing a report on the visit

pages.title: Writing a report on the visit
pages.body:
- Title. For example, A Report on the Handling and Maintenance of Farm Tools at the Farm of Mr Mensah.
- Introduction. State the date, the place, who went and why the visit was done.
- Method. Briefly explain how the observation was done.
- Findings. Present your table and describe the main good and poor practices.
- Discussion. Explain the effect of the good and poor practices on the tools, on safety and on the farm.
- Conclusion and recommendations. Say what the farmer and the community should do better.

Now we use tools safely to do real work in the school garden.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Practising handling for simple farm operations

pages.title: Practising handling for simple farm operations
pages.body:
| **Operation** | **Tool** | **Correct handling** |
|---|---|---|
| Clearing a small plot | Cutlass | Hold firmly, cut away from the body, keep others at least two arm lengths away |
| Loosening and weeding the soil | Hoe | Stand with feet apart, swing the hoe forward and pull it back, keep the blade down when resting |
| Preparing a seedbed | Rake | Pull the rake towards you to level the soil and remove stones, with the teeth facing down |
| Planting seedlings | Trowel and dibber | Make the hole with the dibber, place the seedling and press the soil around it with the trowel |
| Watering | Watering can | Pour gently from a short distance so that the seedlings are not damaged |
| Carrying soil or compost | Wheelbarrow and shovel | Fill to the limit that you can control, and push with a straight back |

After the activity, each group writes down the operational rules they followed. For example, a rule for the hoe could read, Always keep the blade facing down when not in use.

Finally we practise the care steps that keep tools in good condition.

pages.title: Practising maintenance of tools
pages.body:
1. Scrape soil from each tool with a wooden stick and wash it in water.
2. Dry the tool completely with a cloth.
3. Remove rust with sand paper or a wire brush.
4. Sharpen the cutting edge of a cutlass or hoe using a file, moving in one direction at the correct angle.
5. Rub a thin layer of oil or grease on the metal parts.
6. Check the handle for cracks. Tighten loose heads or replace damaged handles.
7. Hang the tools in the tool shed or place them on a rack.
8. Record the rules you used and the tools you have maintained in your notebook.

[[pic: A tidy tool shed. Cutlasses, hoes and rakes hang on hooks on the wall with labels, wheelbarrows stand on a dry floor and buckets are stacked in a corner.]]

> **Safety** Wear boots and gloves while practising. Keep sharp tools pointed down when carrying them. Work in pairs and keep a first aid kit nearby. Never run with tools or play with them.

pages.body:
- Simple crop tools include the cutlass, hoe, pickaxe, shovel, spade, rake, trowel, dibber, watering can and wheelbarrow.
- Simple animal farm tools include feeders, drinkers, brooms, buckets, wheelbarrows, ropes and egg trays.
- Handling is the way a tool is held, used, carried and put down. Maintenance is the care that keeps a tool clean, sharp, safe and working well.
- Good handling prevents accidents. Good maintenance makes tools last longer, saves money and prevents the spread of disease.
- Basic maintenance includes washing, drying, sharpening, oiling, repairing and storing tools in a dry place.
- A farm visit report has a title, introduction, method, findings, discussion and recommendations.
- Each farm operation has its own tool and its own rules, which learners should state and follow.
